articles.title: ‘Sale of govt jobs’ won’t be allowed, says Balochistan CM Bugti
articles.description: QUETTA: Balochistan Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti has warned that no government job in the province will be allowed to be sold, saying that no minister or secretary would be spared if credible evidence of such a practice emerges. Chairing a meeting of the secretaries’ committee on Thursday, CM Bugti ordered an inquiry into complaints of irregularities in recruitment within the forest department. He said anyone found guilty after an impartial investigation would face strict legal action, stressing that the government would not compromise on the employment rights of Balochistan’s youth. The meeting also reviewed provincial departments’ performance and progress under the Annual Development Programme and recruitment procedures. Orders immediate implementation of approved policy for merit-based recruitment through AI Provincial ministers Mir Zahoor Ahmed Buledi and Mir Shoaib Nosherwani, Chief Secretary Shakil Qadir Khan and other officials attended the meeting. The chief minister said the government has made it clear that no job would be sold, adding that the government machinery was united on this policy. He directed officials to ensure transparency and merit in the entire recruitment process and warned that political pressure, favouritism or influence would not be tolerated. He ordered the immediate implementation of the approved policy for merit-based recruitment through AI for all posts from Grade 5 and above, with tests conducted locally and the Chief Minister’s Secretariat providing assistance. He urged officers to perform their duties honestly and impartially. The meeting reviewed progress of development projects. Published in Dawn, September 11th, 2026

articles.title: BOJ hike next week is a given, the real question is pace and terminal rate
articles.description: With a 25bp September hike already fully priced by markets, the actual tradeable content in this report sits in the detail around pace and terminal rate rather than the hike itself. The absence of a preset terminal rate view, combined with an internal split between hawks who see underlying inflation already at 2% and doves like Toichiro Asada, suggests Ueda is likely to keep his post-meeting language deliberately non-committal, which could produce a muted initial JPY reaction even on a confirmed hike. The more market-relevant risk sits with any hint of a faster pace or a larger-than-25bp move, an outcome the sources explicitly downplay given the absence of any sharp overshoot signal in wage or price data. For yen positioning, the tug of war between a yen that's gained over 6% since the July intervention and Brent crude back above $100 a barrel is arguably the more interesting medium-term dynamic than the widely expected hike itself. Earlier: Japan wholesale inflation stays hot in August, cements case for BOJ hike --- The BOJ hikehike next week is old news to markets; the real story is that Ueda has no fixed idea of how far or how fast rates go from here. Summary: Reuters sources say the BOJ is set to raise its policy rate by 25 basis points to 1.25% next week (17 & 18th), taking rates to a 31-year high The central bank is seen having no preset view on the terminal rate, with the pace of further hikes dependent on how prior increases affect the economy and how much of rising input costs firms pass on to households The board is split between hawks who see underlying inflation already at 2% and doves such as Toichiro Asada, who dissented against June's hike Governor Ueda is expected to avoid committing to a specific timeframe for further hikes, though he may repeat earlier comments that the BOJ could speed up tightening if financial conditions are judged too loose Some market players had speculated about a surprise 50bp move, but sources say a larger hike is unlikely given no sign of an abrupt jump in wage or price growth Reuters-polled analysts expect rates to reach 1.5% by end-March 2027 and 1.75% in the second quarter of 2027, with most seeing the terminal rate at 1.75% or higher The Bank of Japan is set to raise interest rates next week, most likely by 25 basis points to 1.25%, according to four sources familiar with the central bank's thinking, a widely anticipated move that markets have already fully priced. The more substantive detail in the Reuters report is not the hike itself but what the central bank is, and isn't, prepared to signal about what comes after it. According to the sources, the BOJ has no preset view on where its terminal rate will ultimately land, with the pace of future increases dependent on how earlier hikes work their way through the economy and on the degree to which firms pass rising input costs on to households. That uncertainty is compounded by a genuine split within the BOJ's board. Some members, described as hawks, believe underlying inflation has already reached the bank's 2% target, while others, including board member Toichiro Asada, who dissented against June's rate increase, remain more cautious. Governor Kazuo Ueda is expected to avoid locking himself into a specific timetable for further hikes at his post-meeting briefing, though he may repeat a July comment suggesting the BOJ could accelerate tightening if financial conditions were judged too loose. Some market participants had floated the possibility of a larger, 50 basis point surprise hike, but the sources say this is unlikely given the absence of any abrupt jump in wage or price growth that would justify a bigger move. That view was echoed publicly on Thursday by BOJ board member Kazuyuki Masu, who said underlying inflation was about to reach 2% but was not showing signs of sharply overshooting that level, a comment read as ruling out an outsized hike next week. The more likely path, per the sources, is the standard 25 basis point increase followed by a period of watching incoming data before deciding on any near-term follow-up. The broader inflation backdrop continues to support the case for tightening regardless of the exact pace chosen. Annual wholesale inflation hit 7.6% in August, which the BOJ expects to feed through into consumer prices in the coming months, and the bank's own July projections point to core consumer inflation reaching 2.5% in the fiscal year ending March 2027. Working in the opposite direction, the yen has gained more than 6% since the joint Japan-US intervention in late July, which would typically ease imported inflation pressure, but that effect is being offset by Brent crude's renewed surge above $100 a barrel. With the September, October, December and January meetings all still to come, the practical takeaway is that markets have a hike essentially locked in for next week, but very little clarity on whether it marks the start of a sustained faster tightening cycle or a single step followed by a longer pause. ---- Dates for the Bank of Japan: This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Smaller Insurers Turn to Industry Veterans
articles.description: South Korea’s small and midsize insurers are turning to seasoned executives born in the 1960s to lead their businesses, putting decades of industry experience to work on company-specific challenges. From left: Park Je-gwang, CEO nominee of DB Life Insurance; Kim Il-pyeong, incoming CEO of LINA General Insurance; and Kim Byung-chul, CEO of KDB Life Insurance. / Courtesy of the companies According to insurance industry sources on September 10, DB Life plans to appoint Park Je-gwang, a former executive vice president of DB Insurance, as CEO following shareholder and board meetings on September 16. Kim Il-pyeong, a former executive vice president of Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance, will take the helm at Chubb-owned LINA General Insurance on September 15. Both companies are entrusting their businesses to former senior executives from major non-life insurers. Park is a DB veteran with 35 years of experience at DB Insurance. Born in Yeongam, South Jeolla Province, in 1963, he graduated from Songwon High School in Gwangju and Seoul National University with a degree in business administration. He joined Dongbu Insurance, now DB Insurance, in 1991 and built his career across corporate sales, new business development, planning and strategy. He became head of new business planning in 2009 and subsequently led the corporate planning and strategic innovation teams. He took charge of the corporate planning office in December 2022. The executive nomination committee recommended him as the next CEO on August 31, setting him up to succeed Kim Young-man, who has led DB Life for six years. Park’s immediate task is to strengthen profitability in the core insurance business. DB Life’s first-half net profit rose 113.5% year on year to 198.1 billion won, driven largely by investment returns. Investment profit jumped 197.5% to 200.1 billion won, while the insurance service result edged up just 1.1% to 54.4 billion won. LINA General’s incoming CEO Kim was born in 1968. He graduated from Yongsan High School in Seoul and earned a degree in statistics from Korea University, followed by a master’s degree in financial engineering from KAIST. After joining Samsung Fire & Marine in 1993, he developed expertise in product design and loss-ratio management, becoming head of automobile product development in 2011 and automobile insurance strategy in 2017. He was promoted to executive vice president in charge of strategic sales in December 2023 before leaving the company in November last year. His experience spans underwriting, product development and distribution strategy. The appointment marks a departure from Chubb’s usual approach. Since 2011, LINA General has largely been led by foreign executives, including Robert Wilkinson, Edward Kopp and Edward Ler. Mo Jae-kyung became its first Korean CEO in September 2023, but he was an internal appointment, having joined the company in 2014. Kim is the first Korean executive recruited from outside the group to lead the insurer. The choice appears to reflect the assessment of Marcos Gunn, Chubb’s regional president for Asia Pacific. Gunn has cited Kim’s deep understanding of the Korean insurance market, supported by his underwriting expertise and experience in strategic distribution expansion and business transformation. Kim is also expected to focus on strengthening the core business. LINA General’s annual net profit fell to roughly 800 million won last year from 35.3 billion won a year earlier. First-half net profit this year recovered to 33.1 billion won, up 3.3 billion won year on year. Turning that recovery into sustained earnings growth will be a key challenge. Organizational changes could add to his agenda. Chubb is targeting the launch of a financial holding company in 2027, while a possible conversion of LINA General from a branch into a locally incorporated subsidiary has also been discussed. KDB Life changed its leadership earlier this year, appointing Kim Byung-chul as CEO. Kim joined the company as senior executive vice president in March last year and was elevated to CEO following an extraordinary shareholder meeting and a board meeting on February 26. His term runs through February 2028. Born in 1969, Kim graduated from Yonsei University and entered the insurance industry in 1999 as a sales manager at Prudential Life. He later served as a branch manager and division head at MetLife and led distribution strategy at ING Life. His career also includes senior roles at OrangeLife, AIA Life and Fubon Hyundai Life, giving him extensive experience in insurance sales and distribution. KDB Life has shown signs of improvement since his appointment. The company returned to profit in the first half, posting net income of 12.9 billion won. Its contractual service margin, or CSM, reached 967.3 billion won at the end of June, up 25.1% from the end of last year. On August 13, Korea Investment Holdings was named the preferred bidder for KDB Life, moving the insurer’s seventh sale attempt into the next stage. The earnings recovery under Kim is seen as helping support the company’s valuation during negotiations. The leadership changes come as smaller insurers face tighter capital requirements. Financial authorities plan to impose prompt corrective measures from next year on insurers whose basic capital ratios under the Korean Insurance Capital Standard, or K-ICS, fall below 50%. Basic capital consists of funds capable of absorbing losses, such as paid-in capital and retained earnings. The requirements could put greater pressure on smaller insurers that have relied on supplementary capital, including subordinated debt, to support their solvency ratios. The recent appointments are being viewed as part of efforts to prepare for the changing regulatory environment. AIA Life is also awaiting a new CEO. Following the recent resignation of Nathan Chuang, Chief Financial Officer and Executive Vice President Jeon Hye-sook has been serving as interim CEO. Chuang reportedly left to join a Hong Kong-based insurer. jdh@chosunbiz.com
